questions.stem: Which situation requires the owner to register a business name with ASIC?
options: Two partners trade using only their own names, Chen and Patel.
A company trades using its exact registered company name.
A sole trader, Mia Chen, trades as 'Fresh Leaf Gardening'.
A sole trader, Mia Chen, trades under her own name, Mia Chen.
questions.explanation: A business name must be registered with ASIC when a business trades under any name other than the owner's own name, the partners' names or the company's exact registered name. 'Fresh Leaf Gardening' is a separate trading name, so it must be registered.

questions.stem: Before registering a business name with ASIC, an owner generally needs:
options: a trade mark registered with IP Australia
a listing on the Australian Securities Exchange
a WorkSafe insurance policy for the owner
an Australian Business Number (ABN)
questions.explanation: An ABN identifies the business to government and is generally needed before a business name can be registered. Trade marks and stock exchange listings are not required to register a business name.

questions.stem: Why does registering a business name with ASIC not, on its own, stop a competitor using a similar brand?
options: Registration gives no ownership of the name; a registered trade mark is needed for that.
Only companies, and not sole traders or partnerships, are able to register business names.
ASIC registers business names only for businesses that sell their goods online.
A registered name is protected only within the owner's own local council area.
questions.explanation: A registered business name lets the owner trade under that name but does not give exclusive rights to it. A registered trade mark with IP Australia gives the legal right to stop others using a similar brand for similar goods or services.

questions.stem: Kai registers 'Peak Brew' as a business name and the domain peakbrew.com.au. A rival in another state begins selling coffee as 'Peak Brew Co'. Kai's strongest protection would have come from:
options: registering further domain names, such as peakbrew.net.au
lodging a complaint with the ATO about the rival's choice of name
registering 'Peak Brew' as a trade mark with IP Australia
registering the business name again separately in each state
questions.explanation: A registered trade mark gives exclusive rights to a brand across Australia for the registered goods and services. Business names are registered nationally but give no ownership, and extra domain names do not stop a rival using the name offline.

questions.stem: A Ballarat florist wants the domain name 'ballaratblooms.com.au'. Which statement about this domain is correct?
options: Once registered, the domain becomes the florist's permanent property and never needs renewal.
Anyone in the world can register a .com.au domain, with no eligibility rules at all.
Registering the domain also registers 'Ballarat Blooms' as a business name with ASIC.
It is registered through an accredited registrar for a set period and must be renewed.
questions.explanation: Australian domain names are registered through accredited registrars for a set term and must be renewed, and .com.au names have eligibility rules requiring an Australian connection. Registering a domain is separate from registering a business name.

questions.stem: Why should a new business register its website domain name early in the planning stage?
options: because a registered domain is required before the business is able to apply for an ABN
because a registered domain gives the brand automatic trade mark protection
because domains can be registered only during a business's first month of trading
so that no one else registers the name first and its brand stays consistent online
questions.explanation: Domain names are allocated to whoever registers them first, so securing the name early protects the business's online identity and lets it match its brand. A domain does not provide trade mark protection, and it is not needed to obtain an ABN.

questions.stem: In Australia, the main trade practices legislation is the:
options: Corporations Act 2001, which regulates the registration of companies
Competition and Consumer Act 2010, which includes the Australian Consumer Law
Fair Work Act 2009, which includes the National Employment Standards
Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004, which covers safety in Victorian workplaces
questions.explanation: The Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) regulates competition and fair trading, and its schedule 2 is the Australian Consumer Law. The other Acts are real and important but deal with employment, workplace safety and companies.

questions.stem: Which body enforces the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 nationally?
options: the Australian Taxation Office (ATO)
the Fair Work Ombudsman
the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC)
the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC)
questions.explanation: The ACCC enforces the Competition and Consumer Act nationally, while state agencies such as Consumer Affairs Victoria also enforce the Australian Consumer Law. ASIC regulates companies and financial services, and the ATO administers tax.

questions.stem: A new juice bar advertises its drinks as '100% organic' when they contain non-organic fruit. Under the Australian Consumer Law, this is:
options: a breach of the Spam Act
misleading or deceptive conduct
unfair dismissal of its employees
an anti-competitive merger or cartel
questions.explanation: Making false claims about the composition of a product is misleading or deceptive conduct, which the Australian Consumer Law prohibits. The juice bar could face penalties and would also damage customers' trust.

questions.stem: A Gold Coast surf shop displays a sign reading 'No refunds under any circumstances'. Under the Australian Consumer Law, this sign is:
options: unlawful, because customers are entitled to a remedy when goods are faulty
lawful, because a business may choose to exclude the consumer guarantees
lawful, provided that the sign is displayed clearly beside the shop's counter
unlawful, because every customer must be refunded for a change of mind
questions.explanation: The consumer guarantees cannot be excluded, so a sign suggesting customers can never get a refund is misleading and unlawful. However, the law does not require a refund when a customer simply changes their mind about a product that is not faulty.

questions.stem: A customer buys a kettle from a new Perth appliance store, and it stops working after two days of normal use. Under the consumer guarantees, the customer is entitled to:
options: a remedy such as a repair, replacement or refund, because it is not of acceptable quality
nothing at all, because the store did not offer any written warranty when it sold the kettle
a remedy only if she returns the kettle to the store within 24 hours of purchase
a remedy only from the kettle's manufacturer and never from the store that sold it
questions.explanation: Goods must be of acceptable quality, and a kettle that fails after two days of normal use does not meet this guarantee, whether or not there is a written warranty. The retailer that sold the goods must provide a remedy; it cannot simply refer the customer to the manufacturer.

questions.stem: A business registered for GST sells a product for $110, including GST. The GST included in the price is:
questions.explanation: GST is 10% of the price before GST, so a GST-inclusive price is 110% of that price and the GST is one-eleventh of it: $110 ÷ 11 = $10. Taking 10% of $110 gives $11, which wrongly calculates GST on a price that already includes it.

questions.stem: A sole trader sells goods for $2,200 including GST and buys stock for $990 including GST. Ignoring all other items, the net GST payable to the ATO is:
questions.explanation: GST collected on sales is $2,200 ÷ 11 = $200, and the GST credit on purchases is $990 ÷ 11 = $90, so the net amount payable is $200 − $90 = $110. Paying $200 ignores the credit the business can claim for GST it has paid on its stock.

questions.stem: A Business Activity Statement (BAS) is lodged with the ATO to report:
options: changes to the business's registered name and contact details
the results of the business's annual customer satisfaction survey
GST and amounts withheld from wages, such as PAYG withholding
the business's compliance with its WorkSafe insurance obligations
questions.explanation: Businesses use the BAS to report and pay tax obligations such as GST and PAYG withholding from employees' wages. Business name details are updated with ASIC, and WorkSafe insurance is dealt with separately.

questions.stem: When a new business begins employing staff, it must:
options: register each employee's name and address with ASIC
lodge its employees' personal tax returns on their behalf
withhold tax from their wages and pay it to the ATO
pay each employee's income tax out of its own profits
questions.explanation: Under PAYG withholding, employers deduct tax from employees' pay and send it to the ATO. The tax is part of the employee's wage, not an extra cost paid from the business's profit, and employees lodge their own tax returns.

questions.stem: A new Bendigo café fails to lodge its BAS and pay the GST it has collected from customers. The most likely consequence is:
options: cancellation of the café's business name registration by the ACCC
the GST becoming the café's own profit once the lodgement deadline has passed
a fine from WorkSafe Victoria for a breach of workplace safety law
penalties and interest charges from the ATO, as well as the unpaid GST
questions.explanation: GST collected from customers belongs to the government, so failing to lodge and pay it leads to ATO penalties and interest on top of the amount owed. The ACCC deals with competition and consumer law, not tax.

questions.stem: In Victoria, WorkCover insurance taken out through WorkSafe Victoria:
options: pays the business's rent if it is forced to close temporarily
covers the costs of compensating workers who are injured at work
covers damage to the business's premises caused by fire or theft
protects the business if a customer sues over a faulty product
questions.explanation: WorkCover insurance pays for injured workers' lost wages and medical and rehabilitation costs. Damage to premises and claims from customers are covered by other types of insurance, such as property and product liability insurance.

questions.stem: Why is WorkSafe insurance a key legal requirement when a Victorian business begins employing staff?
options: It is required only for businesses that operate in the construction industry.
It covers a sole trader's own lost income whenever the business makes a loss.
Employers generally must hold it, so injured workers can be paid wages and medical costs.
It replaces the employer's separate legal duty to keep the workplace safe for all of its workers.
questions.explanation: Victorian employers generally must take out WorkCover insurance so that workers injured at work receive compensation. Insurance does not remove the employer's separate duty under OH&S law to provide a safe workplace.

questions.stem: A new business trades under an unregistered business name, misses its tax lodgements and has no WorkSafe insurance. Which statement best describes the implications?
options: The ACCC will automatically take ownership of the business and its assets.
It risks fines and penalties, damage to its reputation and difficulty obtaining finance.
It faces no consequences until it has been trading for at least three full years.
Only the owner's personal tax affairs are affected, and not the business's day-to-day operations.
questions.explanation: Failing to meet legal requirements can lead to penalties from several regulators, uninsured injury claims and loss of trust from customers and lenders. These obligations apply from the moment the business begins trading or employing.

questions.stem: Which external professional would a new business most likely use for advice on the tax implications of its business structure?
options: a recruitment agent
an accountant
a real estate agent
a graphic designer
questions.explanation: Accountants advise on tax, business structures and financial records. A real estate agent helps find premises and a recruitment agent helps find staff, but neither advises on tax.

questions.stem: Before signing a five-year lease on a shop in Brunswick, the owner of a new bookshop should most appropriately consult:
options: the ATO, so that it can approve the terms of the proposed lease
a lawyer, to check the lease terms and her obligations
an accountant, to register the new lease with ASIC
a bookkeeper, to negotiate the rent with the landlord
questions.explanation: A lease is a legally binding contract, so a lawyer can explain its terms and risks before the owner commits. Leases are not registered with ASIC or approved by the ATO.

questions.stem: Why do many owners use external professionals when establishing a business?
options: External professionals take on legal responsibility for all of the owner's decisions.
The government always pays external professionals' fees on behalf of newly established businesses.
They provide specialist knowledge that reduces the risk of costly legal and financial mistakes.
Using external professionals is a legal requirement for every new business in Australia.
questions.explanation: Lawyers, accountants and other professionals have expertise most new owners lack, helping them comply with the law and set up sound financial systems. The owner remains legally responsible for the business's decisions.

questions.stem: A bookkeeper's main role in a small business is to:
options: design the business's marketing campaigns
choose the business's legal structure
record day-to-day financial transactions accurately
represent the business in court proceedings
questions.explanation: A bookkeeper records transactions such as sales, purchases and payments so that the business has accurate, up-to-date records. Court representation is the role of a lawyer.

questions.stem: Why should a sole trader open a separate business bank account?
options: It keeps business and personal transactions apart, making records and tax easier.
It gives the sole trader limited liability for all of the business's debts.
It means the business no longer needs to keep any receipts or invoices.
It is the only way that a sole trader is able to obtain an ABN.
questions.explanation: A separate account gives a clear record of business income and expenses, which simplifies record keeping and tax returns. It does not change the legal structure, so a sole trader still has unlimited liability.

questions.stem: A café owner requires one staff member to count the cash at closing time and a different staff member to check it against the register total. This is an example of:
options: a business support service
a record-keeping exemption
a financial control system
a customer relations strategy
questions.explanation: Separating the counting and checking of cash between two people is a financial control that reduces errors and theft. Financial control systems are the checks a business uses to protect its money and the accuracy of its records.

questions.stem: Why is accurate financial record keeping important for a new business?
options: It is needed only by public listed companies and not by small businesses.
It ensures that the business will never have to pay any GST to the ATO.
It removes the need for the business to open a separate bank account.
It supports tax compliance and shows whether the business is meeting its financial objectives.
questions.explanation: Accurate records are needed to meet tax obligations and allow the owner to monitor cash flow, costs and profit. All businesses, whatever their size or structure, must keep records.

questions.stem: The ATO generally requires businesses to keep their tax records for:
options: two years
seven years
five years
one year
questions.explanation: Businesses generally must keep tax records for five years, so that the ATO can check them if needed. Keeping records for a shorter period could leave a business unable to support its tax claims.

questions.stem: Which is a sound record-keeping strategy for a new business?
options: using accounting software and storing digital copies of receipts and invoices
keeping receipts only for purchases worth more than $1,000 each
recording transactions once a year, just before the tax return is due
keeping personal and business receipts together in one folder
questions.explanation: Accounting software and digital copies of source documents make records accurate, up to date and easy to retrieve. Recording transactions only once a year leads to errors and gives the owner no current view of the business's finances.

questions.stem: For several weeks, a new retailer's recorded sales have not matched the cash banked, and no single person is responsible for handling cash. The most effective response is to:
options: close the business bank account and keep all of the takings in cash instead
raise prices so that the extra revenue covers the cash that has gone missing
introduce controls such as separating cash duties and reconciling takings each day
stop recording sales altogether, because the existing records are clearly unreliable
questions.explanation: Financial controls, such as clear responsibility for cash and daily reconciliation, make discrepancies easy to detect and discourage theft. Raising prices hides the problem rather than fixing it.

questions.stem: A Hobart restaurant chooses a seafood supplier that delivers on time every day, even though another supplier is slightly cheaper. The restaurant is giving priority to:
options: overseas sourcing
reliability
lowest price
payment terms
questions.explanation: Choosing the supplier that always delivers on time, despite a higher price, puts reliability first. For a restaurant, a missed delivery can mean dishes cannot be served, which may cost more than the price difference.

questions.stem: A planned Melbourne clothing label chooses suppliers that pay fair wages and use recycled fabric. A benefit of this choice is that:
options: it supports the label's CSR objectives and can attract ethically minded customers
it guarantees the label lower costs than any of its less ethical competitors will have
it removes the label's obligations under the Australian Consumer Law
it means the label no longer needs to check the quality of its products
questions.explanation: Suppliers that share the business's values help it meet its CSR objectives and build a reputation that appeals to customers who care about ethics. Such suppliers often cost more, and the business still has all its legal obligations.

questions.stem: A limitation of choosing suppliers that meet a business's CSR objectives is that such suppliers:
options: are not allowed to sell their products to small businesses
always provide lower-quality products than other suppliers
cannot supply businesses located outside their own state
may charge more and can be harder to find or verify
questions.explanation: Ethical and sustainable suppliers may have higher costs, there may be fewer of them, and checking their claims takes time and effort. There is no rule stopping them selling to small or interstate businesses.

questions.stem: A Brisbane café wants to use only Fairtrade-certified coffee. Its current supplier is cheaper but cannot show where its beans come from. Which evaluation is most valid?
options: The choice does not matter, because only manufacturers need to consider who supplies them.
A certified supplier supports the café's CSR goals and reputation, but higher costs may cut its margin.
The cheaper supplier is better, because CSR has no effect on the choices that customers make.
A certified supplier will always reduce the café's total costs over the life of the business.
questions.explanation: A balanced evaluation recognises both the benefit to the café's CSR objectives and reputation and the cost of paying more for certified beans. Many customers do consider ethics when choosing where to buy, so CSR can affect sales.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a policy and a procedure?
options: A policy is required by law in every business; a procedure is always optional and informal.
A policy applies only to the business's managers; a procedure applies only to its customers.
A policy states the business's intentions or rules; a procedure sets out the steps for carrying them out.
A policy sets out the step-by-step method for a task; a procedure states the business's overall intentions.
questions.explanation: A policy is a statement of what the business intends or requires, such as following consumer law on refunds, and a procedure is the set of steps staff follow to put it into practice. The reversed version swaps these meanings.

questions.stem: A new bakery writes a step-by-step method for cleaning its bread slicer safely. This is:
options: a contract between the bakery and its equipment supplier
a procedure that helps it comply with workplace safety law
a policy that sets out the bakery's approach to customers
a business plan that sets out the bakery's financial goals
questions.explanation: A step-by-step method for a task is a procedure, and one for operating machinery safely helps the bakery meet its OH&S obligations. A policy would state the bakery's overall commitment to safety rather than the steps.

questions.stem: Why are policies and procedures important when a business is being established?
options: They help staff comply with legal requirements and set up consistent business routines.
They remove all of the business's legal liability if a staff member breaks the law at work.
They are needed only once the business employs more than 100 staff members.
They guarantee the business will never receive a complaint from a customer.
questions.explanation: Clear policies and procedures tell staff how to act, so legal requirements are met and tasks are done the same way each time. They reduce risk but do not remove the business's legal responsibility for what happens.

questions.stem: A new pharmacy's refund policy says staff must follow the Australian Consumer Law, but there is no procedure telling staff what to do. The most likely problem is that:
options: staff may handle refunds inconsistently, and the pharmacy may breach the law
customers will lose their right to refunds until a procedure has been written
the ACCC must approve a written refund procedure before the pharmacy can trade
the policy is invalid, because every policy must list each step to be followed
questions.explanation: Without a procedure, staff may not know how to apply the policy, so customers could be treated differently or denied remedies they are entitled to. Customers' rights under the Australian Consumer Law exist regardless of a business's internal documents.

questions.stem: A customer database is useful to a new business mainly because it:
options: records the tax obligations that the business owes to the ATO
stores customer details that can be used to tailor marketing and service
replaces the need for the business to register its business name
guarantees that every customer will remain loyal to the business
questions.explanation: A database of customers' details and purchases lets a business contact customers and tailor offers to them. It cannot guarantee loyalty, which depends on the value and service the business provides.

questions.stem: A new Adelaide gift shop wants to email special offers to the customers on its database. Under the Spam Act 2003, it must:
options: have their consent, identify itself and include a way to unsubscribe
send messages only to customers who live in South Australia
pay a fee to the ACCC for each marketing message it sends
include its tax file number in every message that it sends
questions.explanation: The Spam Act requires commercial electronic messages to be sent with consent, to identify the sender and to include a working unsubscribe option. It does not restrict where recipients live or require fees for each message.

questions.stem: What is a key responsibility when a business builds a database of customers' personal details?
options: keeping the information secure and using it only in ways customers would expect
selling the data to other businesses to help cover the costs of setting up
publishing the full list so that customers can see who else shops at the business
deleting the whole database every week so that no legal obligations apply
questions.explanation: Personal information must be protected from misuse and data breaches, and using it in unexpected ways damages trust and may breach privacy law. Selling or publishing customers' details without consent would harm the business's reputation and could be unlawful.

questions.stem: A new Geelong homewares business plans to buy its stock from a supplier in Vietnam. Which issue is it most likely to face?
options: a legal ban on importing any homewares into Australia from overseas
no need to check product quality, because imports are pre-approved
a requirement to register its business name in Vietnam before buying
longer delivery times and costs that change with the exchange rate
questions.explanation: Overseas suppliers usually mean longer lead times, freight and customs costs, and prices that vary as the exchange rate changes. Importers still need to check quality, because they are responsible for the goods they sell in Australia.

questions.stem: A new Australian skincare brand plans to sell through retailers in Singapore and Japan. Which issues should it plan for?
options: no additional issues, because Australian law applies to all of its sales made overseas
only shipping costs, because the overseas retailers will take care of every legal matter for it
only language differences, because exchange rates do not affect businesses that export
different product and labelling rules, time-zone and language differences, and currency risk
questions.explanation: Selling through overseas retailers means meeting each country's product and labelling rules, communicating across time zones and languages, and managing prices that change with exchange rates. Australian law does not govern sales made in other countries.
